question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 20, area 2.) What is the floor of the Class E airspace indicated by the dashed magenta line southeast of Elizabeth City?

options.text: The surface
700 feet AGL
1,200 feet AGL

explanation_correct: A dashed magenta line indicates Class E airspace designated as a surface area for an airport. For Part 107 operations, that means ATC authorization is required because the controlled airspace starts at the surface.

explanation_distractors.B: 700 feet AGL is shown by a shaded magenta vignette, not a dashed magenta surface-area boundary.
explanation_distractors.C: 1,200 feet AGL is the usual Class E transition floor in many areas, but it is not what the dashed magenta boundary depicts.

citation: FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 20

question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 26, area 4 near Jamestown Regional.) The shaded magenta vignette around the airport indicates Class E airspace beginning at

options.text: the surface
700 feet AGL
1,200 feet AGL

explanation_correct: A shaded or fading magenta vignette indicates Class E airspace that begins at 700 feet AGL on the shaded side of the boundary. Below that floor, the airspace is Class G unless another surface-area designation applies.

explanation_distractors.A: A surface Class E area is shown with a dashed magenta boundary, not a shaded vignette.
explanation_distractors.C: 1,200 feet AGL is common elsewhere, but the shaded magenta transition area specifically marks a 700-foot AGL Class E floor.

citation: FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; FAA-CT-8080-2H Figure 26

question_text: METAR: KECG 201253Z 04008KT 10SM FEW035 BKN250 12/08 A3012. What are the visibility and ceiling?

options.text: 10 statute miles visibility and no ceiling
10 statute miles visibility and a ceiling at 25,000 feet
10 statute miles visibility and a ceiling at 3,500 feet

explanation_correct: The METAR reports 10SM visibility. A ceiling is the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), so BKN250 means the ceiling is 25,000 feet AGL. FEW035 does not create a ceiling because a few layer is not considered a ceiling.

explanation_distractors.A: There is a ceiling because a broken layer is present. BKN250 is still a ceiling even though it is high.
explanation_distractors.C: FEW035 is not a ceiling. The lowest broken or overcast layer is BKN250, which is 25,000 feet.

question_text: Pressure altitude is 1,000 feet and the temperature is 35 C. What effect does this high density altitude have on your drone's performance?

options.text: Better climb performance and longer battery life
Reduced propeller efficiency and faster battery drain
No meaningful effect below 400 feet AGL

explanation_correct: High density altitude means thinner air. That reduces propeller efficiency and lift, so the motors work harder to maintain performance. For a small UAS, that usually shows up as weaker climb performance and faster battery consumption.

explanation_distractors.A: High density altitude degrades performance. It does not improve climb or battery endurance.
explanation_distractors.C: Density altitude affects aircraft performance regardless of a Part 107 altitude limit. The air is still less dense at low operating altitudes on a hot day.

citation: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Density Altitude

question_text: You are conducting a Category 3 operation over people. May you fly directly over an open-air concert crowd as part of that operation?

options.text: Yes, if you remain below 100 feet AGL
Yes, if you maintain visual line of sight the entire time
No, sustained flight over open-air assemblies is prohibited for Category 3

explanation_correct: Category 3 operations may not involve sustained flight over open-air assemblies of human beings. A concert crowd is an open-air assembly, so that operation is not allowed under Category 3.

explanation_distractors.A: There is no low-altitude exception that allows Category 3 sustained flight over an open-air assembly.
explanation_distractors.B: Visual line of sight is still required, but it does not remove the open-air assembly restriction.

question_text: A remote pilot is tired after a 12-hour drive and the client is pressuring an immediate small UAS launch so the job can finish before sunset. Which risk-management factors are most clearly present?

options.text: Aircraft only
Pilot fatigue and external pressure
Environment only

explanation_correct: This is a classic risk-management trap. Fatigue falls under the Pilot element of PAVE and the Fatigue item in IMSAFE. Client pressure is External Pressure in PAVE. Both are present and should trigger a no-go or delay decision.

explanation_distractors.A: The described hazard is not primarily an aircraft issue.
explanation_distractors.C: The environment may matter, but the clear immediate risks in the scenario are pilot fatigue and external pressure.

citation: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Aeronautical Decision-Making and Risk Management

question_text: When scanning for aircraft during a civil-twilight or night small UAS operation, which part of the eye is most effective for the remote pilot?

options.text: Cones using direct central vision
Rods using off-center peripheral vision
The cornea only

explanation_correct: Rods are concentrated more toward the periphery of the retina and are much more sensitive in low-light conditions. That is why pilots use off-center viewing at night instead of staring directly at a dim target.

explanation_distractors.A: Cones are best for sharp color vision in brighter light, not for detecting dim objects at night.
explanation_distractors.C: The cornea helps focus incoming light but is not the night-sensitive structure used for scanning.

citation: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Aeromedical Factors

question_text: During flight, the control link between your controller and the drone is lost. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Continue the mission using GPS only and recover the aircraft later
Follow the preprogrammed lost-link procedure and land as soon as practicable
Immediately descend vertically wherever the aircraft is located

explanation_correct: A lost control link is an emergency procedure item. The aircraft should execute its preplanned lost-link response, such as return-to-home or hover-and-land, so the flight terminates as safely as practicable.

explanation_distractors.A: Continuing the mission after a lost control link can create unnecessary risk and is not the standard emergency response.
explanation_distractors.C: An immediate vertical descent may create a greater hazard depending on where the aircraft is. The correct response is the established lost-link procedure.
